en: When I was beating them,
Why did I not die then?
From Alty-Shaar and Kokand,
Six thousand ingots and a thousand otter pelts—
When I was taking tribute from them,
Strutting like a young camel,
When I was swelling with pride,
When the wide world grew narrow,
While Manas, my good fortune, was there,
Why did I not die then?
When I made the age marvel,
When I plundered the Chinese,
Why did I not die then?
When I broke Ombu and took booty,
While my mighty Manas was there,
Breaking through their midst and cutting a road,
When I was mowing them down,
Like a dragon, the world—
When I was sucking it dry,
When Ajybai and Bakai
Were a pair of khans,
When the wide world grew narrow,
While my Sultan Manas was there,
Why did I not die then?!
Untouched by my hand—
How could Margalang have stayed unharmed?
When I threw Jet-Kayt into turmoil,
When I attacked and took Jelpinish,
Why did I not die then?!
Generous Manas, do not die!
Let this wretched soul be spared torment!”
When Ajybai came to Talas,
His head was a bucketful of blood;
His whole body
Was numb and motionless.
He had returned from his errand,
Having lost his beard.
When he arrived in Talas, they looked:
Ajybai had no beard.
That noble woman Kanykey,
When she saw Ajybai,
Stood weeping bitterly,
Stood wailing with piercing cries.
While Kanykey stood weeping,
God had granted the wish:
Your blue-maned Koyonaaly
Had then reached twelve years of age.
He too was a servant beloved of God,
The son Kökbörü had gained when all hope was dying.
His fortune was complete;
Among all the giants upon earth,
He was a truly mighty boy.
To Kanykey, standing in tears,
He came rushing in:
“Mother Kanykey, my father’s sworn brother’s wife,
What sorrow have you?” he said.
“Tell me where your passage is blocked,
Valiant mother Kanykey,
Tell me where trouble has befallen you!
Is there some grievous claim against you?
Is there an enemy come from China?
Without turning aside, mother, tell me the truth!
This year, give me Buurul to ride!
If the foe is of the Khakan’s forces,
I shall drive them into Beijing;
If it is an enemy of Islam,
I shall pursue them all the way to Mecca.
If there is someone of evil intent,
I shall seize them straight before me.
If there is someone fiercely bent on it,
I shall slaughter them as a sacrifice.”
He stood there raging.
The forty champions left by Manas—
He gathered those forty champions;
The forty champions could offer no support:
God had struck them all together.
“Mother Kanykey, my father’s sworn brother’s wife,
Give me the rich cloth coat to wear,
Give me Buurul to ride!
I shall find out about this news.
I shall ride out first and face her:
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
I shall pursue all the way to Mecca.
Without tiring, that bitch Saykal
I shall seize out on the plain.
Just watch the spectacle!
Without tiring, once I seize her,
I shall slaughter her as a sacrifice.
If an army bears us ill will,
If it rages, I shall rout it.
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
I shall seize out on the plain
And make her weep for Khan Manas.
I shall make her tear her face bloody,
I shall make her loose her black hair.
Sparing none alive, I shall make her a widow.
Upon raging Saykal’s
Head I shall tread.
Saykal, who plays the ruler,
I shall seize and crush.
I shall plunder her riches,
I shall bring havoc this year.
On raging Saykal
I shall take vengeance for every distant wrong.
If my appointed hour comes, I shall die;
If I do not die but remain alive,
To Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
I shall go this very year.
If she challenges my fury,
I shall attack her father Karacha.
That old woman who will not take a husband—
I shall drive out her age-old madness.
Give me Buurul to ride,
Mother Kanykey, my father’s sworn brother’s wife!
Give me the rich cloth coat to wear,
Give me Zulpuqor to take!
To beautiful, furious Saykal
I shall go alone myself.”
From the treasury in the palace,
Your formidable sister-in-law Kanykey
Then brought him the rich cloth coat.
With Akkaŋky, the saddle Almambet had made,
She then saddled Buurul for him.
Once he had put on the rich cloth coat,
Once he had mounted Buurul,
Those who saw him were struck with wonder;
The boy looked like a towering mountain,
Gleaming like broad-ringed mail.
When the boy rode, his face shone.
He was twelve years old,
In fighting trim to ravage the Oirats.
He was a lion favored by victory,
His fortune complete.
He rode out, looking about restlessly,
Licking his lips like a hungry wolf.
Upon Buurul, just entering his mature fifth year,
Let us go straight in and speak,
They looked like blue smoke,
Hooves clattering upon the earth,
The black steel bit
Clanging deep in the mouth.
When one looked at Buurul the horse:
A dark roan with a short mane,
Sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs.
When he traveled downhill,
His forelegs struck out like a roe deer’s;
When he came climbing uphill,
His mane and tail streamed out.
When he passed over flint,
It glittered as though a fire were lit.
When he came onto rough ground,
His neck bobbed like a stag’s.
He was a fiery daredevil indeed:
Kökbörü’s only son Koyonaaly
Was twelve years old.
He never shrank back from an enemy,
He never turned back from fire;
He was a fiery daredevil indeed.
His spring flowing down the valley—
Had he not gained him when all hope was dying,
Koyonaaly, Kökbörü’s lamp?
He was a soul of sacred power,
A child born a leopard.
When the champion was born,
The Russians had feasted at his celebration:
“If he lives and grows to manhood,
He will ravage the Oirats,” they had said.
The Chinese had feasted at his celebration:
“If this boy lives,
He will throw the age into turmoil,” they had said.
In the marshland of Mount Jelpinish,
When his mother gave birth to him,
In his right hand, black gold
He came clutching;
In his left hand, red blood
He came holding in his fist.
His coming with black gold clasped in his right hand
Meant: “If there is an enemy bearing ill will,
And take their lives myself.”
His coming with red blood in his left fist
Meant: “If there is an enemy who opposes me,
I shall smash them into red blood
And take their lives myself.”
Leaving Talas, he traveled on,
Covering much ground without sparing his horse.
He spent one night on the way;
The next morning he set out again,
And then he reached the maiden Saykal.
The maiden Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
Looked like a towering mountain;
Unable to stand still for fury,
That bitch had remained
Apart from her forty young men.
When she saw the boy’s distant form,
She took her spear in hand;
Toward the forty young men before her,
She turned and spoke:
“A mist is parting from the sky.
That blue-maned bully Manas
Took it by force before my very eyes;
It was a yearling colt when it went away.
The horse he rides beneath him
Looks like my Buurul!
The finest of my champions,
The ablest of my forty companions,
The strongest of the spearmen,
Hero Bolot, who finds a way—
Turn your horse’s head!
My Bolot, stay in the forward place!
I shall turn Algara’s head;
When he comes among the hills,
I shall shout and level my spear.
I shall knock him down with my spear,
I shall cut off his head,
And Buurul beneath him
I shall seize out on the plain
And add to my horse herd.
I shall strike off his apple-like head,
I shall cut off the wretch’s head.
My Bolot, I shall slaughter him where I catch him,
And the black blood inside him
I shall drink in cupped handfuls until I am full!”
Having said this, Saykal
Strapped on her battle-axe,
Readied Zulpuqor,
Made her Algara strain and pant,
Made him plunge as though her husband had died.
Toward the spur of the rugged mountain,
Toward the crumbling headland,
To the meeting of nine roads,
Raging Khan Saykal,
Parting from her young men,
Flames pouring from her mouth,
Turned her horse’s head.
Saykal stood watchfully.
As for Saykal waiting to intercept him,
The boy sped on, unconcerned.
Of Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
“That is that bitch,” he said.
Your boy did not rate her equal to his trouser cuff;
He passed without counting her a person,
He went without looking back.
Making Buurul surge onward,
The boy passed ahead.
Her thoughts turned to night:
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
Filled inside with boiling rage.
Algara beneath her
She whipped now this way, now that,
Spurring on either side,
Her back hunched behind,
Her eyes glaring ahead,
Her sword ringing in its sheath,
Saykal, Karacha’s daughter,
Came charging with a whir.
She arrived faster than an arrow.
